teaser: Turned down by the jury, hung beside a snack bar, now one of London's most loved paintings.
review_notes:
Rejected by the Salon jury of 1884, then shown at the first exhibition of the Groupe des Artistes Indépendants (May 1884), reportedly hung in the refreshment room / bar: standard account, verify wording.
Preparation: about 14 oil sketches and 10 drawings (National Gallery figures).
Dimensions 201 x 300 cm.
Seurat reworked parts with dots around 1887, including the orange-red hat of the boy on the right: per National Gallery technical studies.
Purchased for the British national collection in 1924 with the Courtauld Fund (first at the Tate, moved to the National Gallery in 1961).
The 'halo' spot (x 0.66, y 0.44): the lighter water beside the central boy's shaded face and chest is visible in the image, but the effect is subtle at this size; check the zoom on the full image.
Claim that the unsold canvas stayed with Seurat until his death in 1891 at age 31.

lesson.text: In the spring of 1884, the jury of the Paris Salon answered a 24-year-old painter with one word: refused. The Salon was the giant official exhibition where careers were made. Georges Seurat had spent about a year on a single canvas for it, and the jury would not hang it.

What he had sent was enormous: 2 meters high and 3 meters wide (about 6.5 by 10 feet). That size was traditionally kept for kings, battles and gods. Seurat used it for a few working men and boys from the edge of Paris, cooling off by the river on a hot day.

Seurat showed the painting anyway, weeks later, at a new exhibition organized by rejected artists, with no jury at all. It was so big that it was reportedly hung in the refreshment room, next to the bar.

The place is Asnières, on the Seine northwest of Paris. On a riverbank in a painting you might expect a pretty countryside. Seurat tells you, far in the distance, exactly what kind of neighborhood this is.
Something on the horizon explains where these bathers probably spend their working week. Can you spot it?

spots.title: Factory chimneys
spots.text: A row of chimneys at Clichy, one sending dark smoke into the summer haze, behind a railway bridge. This is an industrial suburb, and the smoke is painted as tenderly as the sky.

lesson.text: So these are not gentlemen on holiday. The bowler hat, the heavy boots and the plain clothes dropped on the grass belong to workers and shop boys on their time off. Yet nobody splashes or laughs. Each figure sits inside his own silence, solid as a statue.

That stillness was built indoors. Seurat went to the riverbank again and again, making about fourteen small oil sketches on wooden panels and around ten careful drawings of models. Then, in his studio, he assembled the big picture piece by piece, like an architect.
Here is the scaffolding he built his summer afternoon on.

lines.label: The bank
lines.text: The edge of the grass cuts the canvas corner to corner. Land and resting bodies fill one side, water and light the other.

lines.label: The far shore
lines.text: A calm horizontal of bridge, factories and trees steadies the slanting bank, the way a horizon steadies a boat.

lines.label: Steps into the river
lines.text: Three heads go down like stairs: the boy sitting on the bank, the boy waist-deep, the boy in the red hat. Your eye wades into the water with them.

lesson.text: One more thing holds the picture together: nearly everyone faces the same way, to the right, toward the opposite bank. Seurat shows almost every figure in strict side view, like the carved processions on ancient Greek and Egyptian walls that he had studied as a student.
Seurat gave ordinary workers the scale and the stillness that art had reserved for heroes. The subject is modern; the calm is ancient.

He was just as methodical about color. Seurat read scientists who had shown that a color changes according to its neighbor: a pale tone looks paler beside a dark one, and orange looks more intense beside blue. He decided to paint those effects on purpose, with different brushwork for each kind of surface.

lesson.title: Three kinds of touch
lesson.text: Three places where you can see him testing his ideas about color.

spots.title: A halo of water
spots.text: Beside the boy's shaded face and chest, the river turns paler than it is further out. Seurat exaggerates the contrast so the figure stands out from the water without a drawn outline.

spots.title: Crisscross grass
spots.text: The lawn is woven from short strokes going in several directions, greens mixed with yellow and touches of pink. From a distance they blend into sunlit grass.

spots.title: The red hat
spots.text: The hat glows against the blue river because orange-red and blue are opposites. Its surface is speckled with small dots of other colors, unlike the smoother skin beside it.

lesson.text: Those dots on the hat are a later signature. Around 1887 Seurat went back to this canvas and retouched a few areas with the tiny points of pure color that became his famous method, often called pointillism. Bathers is the picture painted just before he invented it.

And the people across the water, the ones the bathers seem to be gazing toward? Seurat painted them next. The opposite shore is the island of La Grande Jatte, where the better-off Parisians strolled on Sundays. His second giant canvas shows that side, entirely in dots.
No one bought Bathers at Asnières during Seurat's lifetime. It stayed with him until he died suddenly in 1891, at only 31, leaving just a handful of large paintings.

Listen to the picture for a second. The only sound in it comes from the boy in the red hat, hands cupped around his mouth, calling out across the river. We never learn to whom, or whether anyone on the other side calls back.

Forty years after the Salon refused it, the painting was bought for the British nation in 1924 with money given by the textile manufacturer Samuel Courtauld. It hangs in the National Gallery in London.

quiz.question: What happened when Seurat submitted the painting to the Salon of 1884?
options: It was bought by the state
quiz.explanation: The official jury rejected it, and he showed it at an exhibition with no jury instead.

quiz.question: What can be seen on the horizon?
quiz.explanation: The chimneys of Clichy show that this is an industrial suburb.

quiz.question: How did Seurat prepare the big canvas?
options: He painted it outdoors in one afternoon
He made small oil sketches and drawings, then composed it in the studio
quiz.explanation: About fourteen oil sketches and ten drawings came before the final picture.

quiz.question: Why does the red hat look so bright?
options: Orange-red and blue are opposites, so each makes the other stronger
It is the only area with thick paint
quiz.explanation: Seurat placed the orange-red hat against blue water to intensify both.

quiz.question: What lies on the opposite bank, toward which the figures face?
options: The island of La Grande Jatte
quiz.explanation: The far shore is La Grande Jatte, the subject of his next big painting.

facts.text: Bathers at Asnières is painted entirely in tiny dots.
facts.explanation: It came before pointillism, and only a few areas such as the red hat were retouched with dots around 1887.

facts.text: The canvas is about three meters wide.
facts.explanation: It measures roughly 2 by 3 meters, a size once kept for grand historical subjects.

facts.text: The painting sold quickly and made Seurat rich.
facts.explanation: It found no buyer in his lifetime and stayed with him until his death at 31.
